content: Emergency medical responders are individuals who have undergone specialized training to deliver medical care outside of a hospital setting during emergencies. Their training can vary significantly, ranging from basic first aid and CPR to advanced life support techniques. The terminology and training requirements for these roles can differ across countries. The term medic is broadly used to describe individuals with varying levels of medical training, from those who provide basic first aid to fully licensed physicians. However, the use of the term does not necessarily indicate a specific level of care or expertise. In some regions, paramedic is used as a general term for medical responders, but it can also refer to a specific level of training. A first responder is typically the first medically trained individual to arrive and provide care to a patient. There are also specific levels of training that fall under the category of first responders. First responders, as a defined level of training, are equipped to perform basic first aid and cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR). In some cases, certified first responders, such as those referred to as community first responders in the United Kingdom, receive additional training in basic life support. These individuals may be laypersons or affiliated with ambulance services. Emergency Medical Technicians (EMTs) represent the next tier of emergency medical providers. In the United States, EMTs are categorized into three levels based on their scope of practice: EMT-Basic, EMT-Intermediate, and EMT-Paramedic (commonly referred to simply as paramedics). Paramedics possess the most advanced training among emergency medical responders and are capable of performing advanced life support procedures. In certain situations, emergency physicians may also respond to critical medical emergencies. Depending on the region, these physicians may operate from ambulances, air ambulances, or specialized response vehicles known as fly-cars. In the realm of wilderness medicine, medical providers receive additional training tailored to the unique challenges of providing care in remote or outdoor environments. Certification levels in wilderness medicine often parallel those of traditional emergency medical responders and include designations such as Wilderness First Responder and Wilderness Emergency Medical Technician. Street medics are individuals who provide medical care during protests or demonstrations. Their medical training varies widely, and they typically serve as volunteers. Flight medics, on the other hand, are usually trained paramedics who have obtained additional certification, such as the Flight Paramedic Certification (FP-C), to operate in aeromedical environments. These professionals work aboard air ambulances. Combat medics are soldiers trained to deliver first aid and trauma care on the battlefield. In the British Army's Royal Army Medical Corps, these individuals are referred to as Combat Medical Technicians. In the United States Army, they are classified under the Military Occupational Specialty code 68W and are known as healthcare specialists.
